newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Afghan war focus shifts to far northwest.
newsitem.headline: Afghan war focus shifts to far northwest.

text.p: The focus of Afghanistan's war shifted to the remote northwest on Friday with the battle for Kabul apparently at a stalemate, reliable sources said.
"We'd really like to know what's going on up there, but independent reports are few and far between," said one.
Both the purist Islamic Taleban militia, now ruling three-quarters of Afghanistan, and a northern alliance arrayed against it claimed control of Badghis province on Thursday.

The alliance's Radio Afghanistan, monitored by the British Broadcasting Corporation (BBC), said its forces had taken the whole of Bagdhis and were pushing into neighbouring Herat province, which borders Iran.

Acting Information Minister Amir Khan Mutaqi told reporters on Thursday it was the Taleban who controlled Bagdhis, but his assertion appeared to contradict a Taleban spokesman in the western city of Herat.

He told the Pakistan-based Afghan Islamic Press on Wednesday there had been heavy overnight fighting in Bagdhis, a day after reliable sources in Kabul said the alliance forces were moving on the provincial capital of Qalaye-i-Naw.
Afghan watchers said they also had reliable reports of the Taleban being driven back in Bagdhis earlier in the week, but had heard nothing since.

If the forces of Uzbek leader Abdul Rashid Dostum, allied against the Taleban with former government military chief Ahmad Shah Masood, had pushed into Herat, then the whole complexion of the war could change, the Afghan watchers said.
"If Dostum can take Herat, then the Taleban are in trouble," said one.

Herat, which has a large population of Tajiks who are cousins to Masood's people, lies on plains running all the way to the southern city of Kandahar, where the largely ethnic Pashtun Taleban have their headquarters.
"The Taleban went from Kandahar to Herat in four days last year. The alliance may not be able to do that, but they can threaten the Pashtun heartland," an Afghan watcher said.
"It will also be interesting to see at what point Ismael Khan enters the picture," he said of the former governor of Herat who belongs to Masood's party.
"There have been rumours that he is moving back in from Iran and it is a logical move," he added.
Khan was present in Dostum's capital of Mazar-i-Sharif when the Uzbek leader and Masood finalised their military pact last month.
The alliance has made little progress in a series of heavy assaults on Taleban lines in hills 25 to 30 km (15 to 19 miles) north of Kabul in the past 10 days.
Masood and Dostum made their latest attempt to break through the hills and onto the plains of the Shamali valley leading down to Kabul on Thursday.
Taleban fighters near the front line said on Friday the assault had not changed the front lines. The fighting had reverted to long-range artillery exchanges, they said.
Thursday morning's assault was followed by two Dostum bombing raids on the capital in which three children were killed and seven people wounded.

Five bombs fell, three of them near the airport on the northeast edge of the city and two more, which caused the first war casualties in Kabul since the Taleban took over in late September, several kilometres (miles) away.
An Afghan watcher with a military background said the two bombs were probably aimed at a nearby military base.

One of the bombs, a 500 kg (1100 lb) fuel-air bomb, according to experts, failed to go off. The other landed in a field about 400 metres (yards) from the airport, which is used for both civilian and military traffic.
